entries.question: What are the key tax changes affecting property investors right now?
entries.answer: Based on the retrieved transcripts, the key tax changes affecting property investors are: (1) major CGT changes for existing residential property — properties (other than brand-new post-budget builds) will need a market value as at 1 July 2027, with a 50% CGT calculation up to that value and then an indexation cost-base calculation [3]; (2) a flat 30% trust tax on distributions to beneficiaries, plus an extra tax on distributions to corporate beneficiaries / "bucket companies," which may result in double taxation [3]; (3) a minimum 30% tax on real capital gains regardless of marginal tax bracket, described as damaging for lower-income investors such as non-working spouses and younger lower-income investors [3]; (4) tax brackets were not indexed, meaning as investors earn more they will face bracket creep [9]; (5) "mum and dad" investors are most impacted through negative gearing losses and the 50% CGT exemption in personal names, while sophisticated investors using company structures see less impact [1][2]; and (6) at the top marginal bracket the difference between the 50% CGT exemption and a flat 30% tax is about 6.5%, or $65,000 extra tax on a $1 million gain [6]. The largest changes are said to target existing residential property [4].

entries.question: If I bought an investment property before budget night, do I keep negative gearing?
entries.answer: Yes. If you owned the property before budget night (12 May, 7:30 p.m.), your existing property remains as is and you keep negative gearing benefits on that existing portfolio, regardless of whether the property is old or new [4]. In the transcript, it is stated: 'anyone who owns properties pre-budget, firstly, those properties remain as is' [2], and existing properties are described as being under the 'grandfathered negative geared provision' [1].

entries.question: What is now the best property strategy for investors post budget?
entries.answer: The retrieved chunks do not prescribe one single 'best' strategy; the advice is that the right move depends on your situation. For newer/individual investors, the recommendation is to buy your first one or two properties in your own name, keep it low-cost and simple, and hold long-term with an exit in mind, because the indexation method rewards longer holding and is not suited to short-term flips [1][8]. For existing investors, the speakers strongly advise against selling 'grandfather' properties acquired pre-budget, since those keep their existing treatment and selling would forfeit tax benefits [3][7]. More sophisticated investors may need to consider company structures, while trusts have lost some investment luster but can still be used as shareholders of companies to distribute fully franked dividends later [1][8]. The speakers also caution against knee-jerk moves such as jumping into commercial property solely because of budget changes—commercial carries tenant vacancy risk and, if you occupy it, business risk—so get advice and keep a solid portfolio foundation [4]. Overall, one speaker says the budget changes little for sophisticated investors and hits mom-and-dad investors hardest, and negative gearing is not gone; pre-budget properties are grandfathered [7][10]. All of this is general information, not personal financial advice [9].

entries.question: Is the Gold Coast property market at risk of collapse, and why?
entries.answer: The Gold Coast-specific speakers express serious concern that the market could be hit harder than any other, but this is opinion rather than a data-backed collapse forecast [3]. They cite: the Gold Coast's history as a volatile boom-and-bust, lifestyle/holiday-driven market [2]; COVID-era population moves reversing as people returned to their home cities [2]; a wave of off-the-plan penthouses, marketing hype, and 'spruikers', including buyer's agent institutes [3]; extreme supply swings, with vacancies oscillating from 0.5% to 9% over a cycle [3]; and the structural risk of buying off-plan 3 years before settlement, where a buyer can be 20% down on settlement day, with valuation risk and potential deposit loss [10]. Because of that, the speakers advise buying 'acute resales' in completed buildings rather than new off-plan contracts, since you know the current market and real price at purchase [1].

entries.question: Summarise the key insights from the Suburb Data episode on what is happening across Australia's property markets.
entries.answer: Damian and Jeremy open the Suburb Data episode by explaining they review their platform's monthly data (usually released around the 6th) and look at metrics such as stock on market, days on market, vacancy rates, typical values, and the DSR/market cycle timing [2][3][10]. Over the past year most capital-city markets have picked up: Darwin and Perth are the high flyers, with Hobart, Brisbane and Adelaide also running well, while Canberra, Melbourne and Sydney lag; even within lagging cities there are hot pockets—Sydney has roughly 700 suburbs and Melbourne about 500 [1][2]. The hosts expect the next 1–2 months of data to begin reflecting proposed CGT and negative gearing changes [2]. Stock on market has picked up almost everywhere following the federal budget announcement, with Darwin rising fastest [1][5]. Days on market has increased about 6% across most cities (for example, roughly 34 to 39 days), but the market remains tight versus the normal expectation of about 60 days [4]. Vacancy rates are very tight, especially in Darwin, which dropped from 0.6% to 0.3% (and later 0.4% for its small unit market) [4][7]. The hosts argue federal tax changes won't alleviate rental pressure: established properties will increasingly sell to owner-occupiers rather than investors, reducing rental supply and pushing rents up until cash-flow-positive property brings investors back [5]. On typical values, Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide were the main monthly movers, Melbourne moved up after DSR 3 algorithm adjustments, and the team is waiting on a full month of June data to see the post-announcement trend [10].

entries.question: tell me the most effective AI coding setup to build an app with agentic coding that doesn't suffer from ai slop and is scalable
entries.answer: No single 'most effective' setup is directly compared in the retrieved chunks, but they converge on a few principles: use a model-agnostic agent harness with a smooth out-of-the-box experience (OpenCode is highlighted) [2]; learn to build agents from scratch in Python before reaching for frameworks like LangChain/LangGraph/Pydantic AI, so you don't treat them as magic [10]; and route production LLM calls through enterprise providers like AWS/Azure/GCP for centrally managed billing, data privacy controls, and scaling [5]. To avoid 'AI slop' (framed here as unmaintainable code), keep a human in the loop and do 'program design' before letting the agent run, because agents will make decisions you might not like and won't write maintainable code alone [7]. For harder tasks, you can assemble agent teams rather than relying on a single agent [1], and the agentic loop should use tools to search your codebase and relevant knowledge [4].

entries.question: Describe the Agentic Engineering Workflow: every step and what it leverages.
entries.answer: Based on the retrieved chunks, the agentic engineering workflow is a human-directed, agent-executed pipeline. It starts with a human deciding what to build and a system/agents figuring out how to build it [7]. Before agents 'cook,' program design is done: you specify measurable outputs and how you want the work done, because otherwise agents make decisions you may not like [6]. The workflow then assembles the core setup ('ship'), recruits and ramps crewmates using memory and skills, works with a single crewmate, scales to multiple simultaneous crewmates, and adds a first mate to manage overhead [5]. In the design phase, all decisions are written down, the agent plans/schedules and sequences work (e.g., schema changes before web changes, separate work trees), and then lane cards are written and a 'compact' is done before building starts [4]. Build execution replaces 'person builds the thing' with 'agent builds the thing,' leveraging orchestration, harness, sandbox, and model components; humans still review code by hand and loop failures back [3]. For long-running work, it leverages multi-agent patterns—delegation, creator-verifier, broadcast, and negotiation—combined into a mission where you describe a goal, scope it through conversation, approve a plan, and orchestrator/worker/validator agents execute via structured handoffs and shared state [7][8]. Agents use an agentic loop with tools to search codebases and general knowledge, steered by additional instructions/domain knowledge [10]. It is also framed around context engineering—Dexter invented the term—and the design phase explicitly tracks context usage before building [6][4]. Finally, the human stays in charge because the agent 'educates' you with quizzes, HTML visualizations, and by slowing down when you lose grip [9].

entries.question: How do I set up Herder, and what app do I run it in?
entries.answer: To set up Herder, add it to your Homebrew configuration (in configuration.nix) as a normal brew formula, not a cask, then create its configuration directory and create a config file at config.toml, pasting your config in [1]. Herder is a terminal multiplexer, so you run it from your terminal, and the transcript notes it might be the only terminal multiplexer that works on Windows too [1]. The retrieved chunks do not name a specific terminal emulator app to run it in.

entries.question: How should I use memory files and skills to onboard a coding agent?
entries.answer: To onboard a coding agent, combine two mechanisms: memory files and skills. Set up a global memory file that all agents read, plus a project-level memory file, and share them across harnesses by symlinking the canonical file (e.g., CLINE.md -> AGENTS.md) so every agent uses identical memory [1][9]. In the project memory file, store project context, repo layout, terminology, component explanations, end-to-end testing instructions, and conventions; build it incrementally by correcting the agent when it errs and asking it to record the lesson [2]. Keep it as plain markdown—no fancy memory system needed [2]. To prevent bloat, move conditionally useful content (like end-to-end testing steps only relevant on code changes) out of the memory file and into skills [2][3]. Skills support progressive disclosure: only a short description is loaded into the system prompt initially, and the full body is read only if the skill is needed, saving tokens [7]. If your harness doesn't know how to create skills, install Anthropic's skill-creator via the Vercel `npx skills` CLI [3]. Finally, enforce consistent behavior across all agents with a global memory file of preferences (e.g., no em-dashes, no auto co-author attribution) [4]. Be cautious about installing third-party skills from the internet—they can run arbitrary commands and leak your API keys [7].

entries.question: What are the main themes across this corpus of videos?
entries.answer: The corpus contains several distinct, loosely connected themes. One theme is AI-assisted media/software production: a sports-footage pipeline that transcribes audio, generates text/video embeddings, matches behaviors to vectors/confidence, stores them, and sends notifications [1][2], alongside workflows where pre-built UI components are copied and handed to an AI agent to install [3]. Another theme is premium app design and craft: noticeable differences in animation effort, using Mobin to study good animations frame-by-frame [4], iterating with AI agents through dictation tools like Whisper Flow [7], and concluding that 'taste' is a defining skill and 'premium is felt more than seen' [5]. A third theme is career/job-search advice: emphasizing impact over generic projects, finding whose pain to solve [10], and resume professional-summary examples/templates [8]. Finally, there is a conference-talk segment pointing to Databricks Summit sessions and additional resources [9]. Overall, the videos share loose threads around AI-assisted workflows and personal/career development, but they are not one continuous narrative.

entries.question: What are the recurring arguments the property videos make about the federal budget's tax changes?
entries.answer: The videos repeat several recurring arguments: the budget bundles measures such as negative gearing restrictions, capital gains tax indexation, trust/bucket-company changes, and the WATTO into one package that mainly hurts 'mum and dad' investors, rentvestors, and families, not sophisticated investors who already use trusts or forego some benefits [3][10]. They call it a 'tax grab' that will not help the property market because population growth, housing demand, and the tax load on new builds (estimated at 30–50% of a house-and-land package) remain unchanged [2][6]. They also argue investors will find 'other mechanisms and ways to get around' the changes, and that selling grandfathered properties would forgo tax benefits [2][4]. Another repeated point is that the policy is confusing: negative gearing changes are deferred until the 2028 tax return, negative gearing losses are deferred rather than gone, the CGT discount still applies, and indexation is only a new calculation method [9]. Finally, a broader argument is that the budget shows 'everything is up for grabs,' so investors should do doomsday planning, and that rents will rise far more than the government's $2-a-week estimate [7][8].

entries.question: According to this corpus, how do senior engineers structure their agentic coding setups?
entries.answer: The corpus's senior practitioners describe a layered, human-led setup. They start with a core setup, recruit and ramp up "crew mates" using memory and skills, work with a single crew mate first, then scale to multiple crew mates and add a "first mate" that manages overhead so the human stays the captain [7]. Concretely, they keep memory files like agents.md and ask the agent to convert conditionally useful information into project-level skills, using the npx skills CLI and Anthropic's skill creator where needed [3]. They set up agents with parameters, additional instructions, and domain knowledge, and rely on an "agentic loop" where the model searches the codebase and other information sources [1]. At the workflow level, they run a software-factory-style loop in which an agent replaces the "person builds the thing" step, while human review and CI/CD remain [4]. They also apply context engineering, especially the principle of "own your context window" [5]. For multi-agent work, they use patterns like creator-verifier (a fresh agent reviews the builder's work), direct communication, negotiation over shared resources, and broadcast [6]. Finally, they keep the human in charge: agents should educate the user and slow down so the human does not lose touch with the codebase [8].

entries.question: How did the property channels' stance on the budget's tax changes evolve across June 2026?
entries.answer: The retrieved chunks contain no evidence of an evolution in the property channels' stance across June 2026. They present a consistent, largely skeptical post-budget position: the hosts call the package a 'tax grab' [7], emphasize that investors will not feel the negative gearing change until the July 2028 tax return at the earliest [2][4], stress that the change is 'deferred versus gone' rather than repealed [4], warn that 'everything is up for grabs' and 'no one's coming to save you' [9], and advise worst-case planning [9]. The only reference to June 2026 in the provided chunks is an example purchase date whose first affected tax return is July 2027 [8] — not a window in which the speakers' stance is shown to shift. Without additional chunks covering commentary across that period, no evolution can be traced.

entries.question: How do I make my resume ATS-friendly?
entries.answer: Make your resume ATS-friendly by keeping the layout simple and machine-readable. Use Google Docs or Word and export a PDF, because PDFs preserve formatting and are safer than Word or Google Doc files [1][4]. Avoid graphics editors, colors/highlights, tables, footers, headers, images, emojis, symbols, and multi-column layouts, since these can confuse ATS parsing or be read out of order [4][6]. Use an easy-to-read font such as Arial, Calibri, or Garamond, keep body text around 10 pixels, and keep margins consistent (one inch, reducing to half an inch if needed) [4][6]. Organize your resume into clear sections: a header with your name, role, LinkedIn/GitHub, and location, plus a logically grouped skills section [9]. Then keyword-optimize by pulling the most important terms from the job description into your summary, skills section, and bullet points [1][5][2]. You can use an AI tool like ChatGPT with a prompt to generate the 25 most important keywords for the job, then weave them into your resume [8][2]. Tailor the summary per application so it echoes the job title, e.g., 'senior front-end engineer' instead of 'front-end developer' [7]. Finally, remember ATS rejects a large portion of resumes—about 75% in one study [3] and 70-80% per an experienced reviewer [10]—and a recruiter may spend only 6-8 seconds after that [9][10], so make it a keyword-scannable sales pitch.

entries.question: What should the professional summary at the top of a resume say?
entries.answer: A resume professional summary should quickly tell hiring managers who you are and what you can do for them—not just restate your objective of finding a job [2]. Keep it short, around one to two sentences max [8], and make it specific to the job: lead with your professional role, years of experience, and the environments you've worked in, then use the second sentence to brag about specific accomplishments, ideally with facts and figures showing results from previous roles [2][3]. Avoid generic buzzwords or boilerplate you wouldn't customize per application [8]. For career changers or new professionals, the summary should instead show eagerness to learn and concrete effort to master the new field [4][7]. Write it last, after the rest of the resume is done, so it genuinely summarizes what's on the page [6].

entries.question: How should I write my LinkedIn about section and skills so recruiters find me?
entries.answer: To make your LinkedIn profile discoverable to recruiters, think of LinkedIn search as keyword-based: recruiters type titles/skills into LinkedIn search, so the right keywords determine whether you appear high in results [1][6]. Start by copying 5–10 job descriptions for your target role into a document and pasting them into a word cloud generator to identify the most frequent keywords [1]. Use those keywords in your About section, written as 3–4 concise paragraphs: (1) introduce yourself with years of experience, roles, and technologies; (2) write a compelling summary that highlights skills, experience, and career goals with numbers/data; (3) close with the types of opportunities you want [1]. Keep your headline short and specific using a role + skill/interest + value proposition template, and avoid generic filler words [3]. Place your chosen keywords in the About, Experience, and Skills sections, and in your header/bio, because keywords in multiple places increase visibility [2][6]. For the Skills section, pull the same job-description keywords (or use an AI prompt to extract hard skills, technologies, job functions, industry terminology, and leadership skills) and add as many relevant skills as needed from the 100-skill limit, while avoiding repetitive entries [7][9]. LinkedIn only counts skills that have at least one endorsement, and you need five endorsed skills to fully use the Skills section, so ask colleagues/friends/classmates to endorse your top five target skills [4]. You can also upload your resume via Settings & Privacy > Data Privacy > Job-seeking preferences > Job application settings to help you surface for the same keywords [2]. Finally, in your written descriptions, emphasize impact with metrics (e.g., 'led a team of 10 to increase sales by 15%') instead of listing duties, because past results signal future performance to recruiters [10].

entries.question: What does a recruiter actually look for on an AI engineer resume?
entries.answer: A recruiter looks first for qualifications, not keyword matches: for an AI engineer role, the must-have list includes AI, LLM, NLP, Python (or C/Java, Python preferred), agentic frameworks like LangChain/Crew, MCP/A2A, generative AI/RAG, ML frameworks like TensorFlow/PyTorch, API design, Git/GitHub, cloud, NumPy/R/MATLAB, SDLC/CI/CD/DevOps, and the ability to explain things to non-technical people; a candidate generally needs 75% of these, and they cannot just live in a skills section [2]. Recruiters and engineers also value specialization, actual daily work-experience depth (e.g., "ReactJS" meaning real on-the-job use, not just dabbling), and stand-out signals like open-source contributions [1]. Practically, a skills section is often a waste of space—the top "North Star" project should lead the resume and make skills self-evident [5][6]. Career-changers should reframe previous experience (e.g., scalable, fail-safe systems) around one clear AI/data pipeline project, and keep the resume to one page [3][7][9]. The resume should also be written in a parseable format like LaTeX or markdown so an AI agent can fact-check it for each application [7].

entries.question: How should I prepare for behavioural interview questions?
entries.answer: To prepare for behavioural interviews, practice in advance and try to predict the questions that will come up [3]. Build a reusable story bank of about five or six stories and frame your answers using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) [1]. For Amazon specifically, map your answers to leadership principles like bias for action, ownership, and customer obsession [1]. Use a template (for example, a Notion tracker) to prepare answers to common questions like “Why do you want to work here?” and “Tell me about a conflict,” and refresh old stories using your current work summary [2][7]. Practice by reciting your answers aloud, ideally to a mirror or camera [7]. Don’t talk yourself out of stories that feel too small, because you are usually more critical of yourself than the interviewer [6]. After each interview, write down the questions you were asked and your answers to build and refine your bank over time [6]. Finally, prepare thoughtful questions to ask at the end, such as what a successful new hire looks like on the team [6].

entries.question: What advice do the job-search videos in this corpus repeat across resumes, LinkedIn and interviews?
entries.answer: Across the chunks, the clearest repeated advice is to tailor your materials to the specific jobs you are targeting. On resumes, [9] advises making your resume as fitting as possible to a role and its required skills, and [10] warns that a tech-stack mismatch with the job description can get a resume thrown out. On LinkedIn, [7] says to mine job postings for the skills, software, and industry terminology they mention and add those to your profile, while [5] says to update your profile with new skills and specify the types of roles and locations you want. The other repeated theme is to avoid the high-volume, standard application 'black hole': [1] promises to show how to apply "so we don't end up in a black hole," [6] explicitly advises against applying to 50 jobs a day, and [2] reports that standard applications via LinkedIn had a low interview success rate and that a different approach had a much higher success rate. As for interviews specifically, the only retrieved evidence is [1]'s promise to cover how to prepare for and nail every job interview; none of the provided chunks contain actual interview advice.

entries.question: What are the key tax changes affecting property investors right now?
entries.answer: Based on the retrieved transcript chunks, the key tax changes described are: reduced benefits from negative gearing and the 50% capital gains tax (CGT) exemption for 'mom and dad' investors, while sophisticated investors using structures are expected to be less affected [1][2]. For existing (non-brand-new) properties, a market value must be done at 1 July 2027 with a 50% CGT calculation up to that value and an indexation cost base after that date [3]. The budget also introduces a 30% flat tax on trustees, plus an extra tax on distributions to corporate 'bucket company' beneficiaries that could result in double taxation [3], and a minimum 30% tax rate on real capital gains even for lower-income taxpayers [3]. Tax brackets were not indexed for future years, meaning bracket creep will occur [9]. One speaker estimates that the CGT difference at the top bracket is about 6.5%, e.g., an extra $65,000 tax on a $1 million gain [6], and expects the biggest market impact to be on existing residential property [1][4].

entries.question: If I bought an investment property before budget night, do I keep negative gearing?
entries.answer: Yes. Properties held before budget night (12 May, 7:30pm) keep their negative gearing benefits, and the new restrictions apply to properties bought after that point [4]. Pre-budget properties remain unchanged, so investors can still claim negative gearing on those existing holdings [2][3].

entries.question: What is now the best property strategy for investors post budget?
entries.answer: There is no single 'best' strategy in the transcript; the advice depends on investor type. The speakers split investors into existing investors and new starters [5]. Existing investors should hold on to 'grandfather' properties rather than sell because selling would forfeit tax benefits [3]. New investors are told to buy their first one or two properties individually, keep costs low and simple, buy with an exit in mind, and expect to hold long-term as income and borrowing capacity grow [1][8]. Negative gearing is not 'gone' in the immediate sense: pre-budget properties remain as they were, and a June 2026 purchase would still show the same outcome in the July 2027 tax return [7]. For more sophisticated investors, structures such as companies are worth considering now, while trusts have lost some investment luster (though still useful in certain setups), with planning rates now more in the 30–47% band [8]. The speakers also caution against knee-jerk decisions, advise getting specialist advice before moving into commercial/high-yield assets [4][6], and describe tax as a cost of success to be minimized within the new rules [2][10]. Overall, the budget is said to change little for advanced investors but to affect 'mom and dad' investors most [10].

entries.question: Is the Gold Coast property market at risk of collapse, and why?
entries.answer: Yes — the speakers express serious concern that the Gold Coast market could get “smashed harder than any” [3]. Reasons cited in the transcript include: (1) Gold Coast has historically been a volatile boom-and-bust market, with cycles driven by lifestyle demand before COVID [2]; (2) COVID-era migration from city buyers appears to be reversing, with migration data showing people heading back to Melbourne and their existing family/obligations [2]; (3) the market is described as a “supply height market” with brutal supply swings, including vacancy rates swinging from 0.5% to 9% over a cycle [3]; (4) off-the-plan purchases are signed 3 years before settlement, which exposes buyers to valuation risk and potential deposit loss if the property is worth 20% less by settlement [10]; and (5) the safer advice given by one speaker is to look for resales rather than buying off the plan, because resales reflect the market at the time of purchase [1]. So the risk is attributed to speculative off-the-plan buying, supply/demand volatility, and the unwinding of temporary COVID-driven demand, rather than a single structural cause.

entries.question: Summarise the key insights from the Suburb Data episode on what is happening across Australia's property markets.
entries.answer: Hosts Damian and Jeremy review monthly Australian capital-city property data around the 6th of each month, looking at stock on market, days on market, typical values, vacancy rates, and DSR as a timing metric [2][3][10]. Over the past year Darwin and Perth were the strongest capital markets, with Hobart, Brisbane and Adelaide also performing well, while Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra lagged [2]. In the most recent month, Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra and Adelaide gave back some ground overall, but the hosts stress there are still hot pockets and that Sydney/Melbourne's higher typical values may make them feel the slowdown more [1]. Stock on market rose almost everywhere, notably in Darwin; Hobart and Adelaide were the exceptions [1][7][10]. Days on market lifted around 6% (e.g., 34 to 39 days), which is noticeable but still tight relative to the usual ~60 days [4][7]. Rental markets remain extremely tight: Darwin vacancy tightened from 0.6% to 0.3% (0.4% in a later read), and Brisbane, Hobart, Adelaide and Perth were also low [4][7]. The hosts expect federal CGT and negative-gearing changes to flow into data over the next 1–2 months, reduce rental supply in established areas as properties go to owner-occupiers, and push rents up until cash-flow-positive returns bring investors back [2][5]. In related discussion, listings are up 22% year-on-year and the hosts warn of a potential massive rental boom and a worrying two-class economy [6]. They also caution that markets with long growth runs and heavy reliance on negative gearing could tank or flatline for a decade, citing Sydney's 2003–2013 flat run and Brisbane/Perth/Adelaide's 2007–2020 stagnation [9].

entries.question: tell me the most effective AI coding setup to build an app with agentic coding that doesn't suffer from ai slop and is scalable
entries.answer: Based only on the retrieved chunks, there is no single fully specified "most effective" setup, but the evidence points to a combination of practices. The chunks don't explicitly define "AI slop," but they discuss the same risk as agents producing unmaintainable or "terrible" code [4]. To counteract that, do program design before letting the agent work: specify a measurable output and tell the model how you want it done, then keep the human in the loop with checkpoints, quizzes, and visualizations so you don't lose touch of the codebase [4][6]. For the agent harness, Open Code is highlighted as model-agnostic with a smooth TUI and a complete out-of-the-box feature set, while Codex CLI is smoother and open source so the agent can inspect its own source code [1]. For scalability, keep the AI layer simple — use direct API calls or enterprise endpoints on AWS/Azure/GCP for centralized billing, data privacy, and scaling [3], and avoid unnecessary new tooling because the AI layer is typically just API calls [8]. Also, agent-facing tool design matters: a benchmark in the chunks shows that using the GitHub MCP server costs about 3x more in tokens and more than double the latency versus using the CLI, and agent-first design standards like AXI can reduce token usage by about 40% [10]. The chunks also reference Dave Ablar's preferred five-layer stack for AI automations — Python backend, frontend, AI layer, and infrastructure — but the full architecture, especially the infrastructure layer, is not explained in the retrieved material [2][7].

entries.question: Describe the Agentic Engineering Workflow: every step and what it leverages.
entries.answer: Based on the retrieved chunks, the agentic engineering workflow is described as: (1) assemble the core setup and "recruit/ramp up crew mates" using memory and skills, then progress from one agent to multiple agents and finally a "first mate" that manages overhead [5]; (2) before building, do program design — specify measurable outputs and tell the agent how you want the work done, because the agent otherwise makes decisions you might not like [6]; (3) have the agent write up decisions and plan the sequence of work, including schema changes, separate work trees, lane cards, and a "compact" before building [4]; (4) replace the human "build the thing" step with an agent that builds in minutes or hours, leveraging orchestration, harness, sandbox, and model infrastructure, while keeping human code review, CI/CD, production, monitoring, and user-feedback loops from the pre-AI software factory [3][10]; (5) keep the human in charge by having the agent educate you with quizzes/visualizations and slow down when you lose grip [7]; (6) convert conditionally useful memory into skills, using tools like Anthropic's skill creator and Vercel's npx skills CLI so agents can create new skills [8]; and (7) bring human intuition into the loop early instead of reviewing a 2000-line feature at the end [9].

entries.question: How do I set up Herder, and what app do I run it in?
entries.answer: Herder is a terminal multiplexer that you run inside a terminal emulator — the video uses WezTerm (transcribed as 'Westerm') as that terminal app after closing the default macOS Terminal [1][10]. To set it up, add Herder to your Homebrew configuration in your Nix configuration.nix file (as a brew package/cask), create Herder's config directory and a config.toml file (the transcript shows keybinds that preserve tmux muscle memory), create a symbolic link so the config applies, and then rebuild Nix. After that, you can launch Herder from the terminal, which shows a side panel for workspaces/agents and a main terminal area [1][9].

entries.question: How should I use memory files and skills to onboard a coding agent?
entries.answer: Onboard coding agents through two mechanisms—memory files and skills—so fresh agents learn how you run your project and how you like to work [1]. Use a minimal global memory file (e.g., AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, often symlinked) that sits in the system prompt for every agent session across all projects; keep it short because everything in it consumes tokens on every request [1][4][10]. Put personal rules there such as 'never use em-dash' and 'don't auto-add your agent's name as co-author' [4][10]. Then keep a project-level memory file (CLAUDE.md/agents.md) containing repo layout, terminology, how key components work, end-to-end testing instructions, and conventions; build it over time by correcting mistakes and asking the agent to store those learnings [2][9]. To prevent that file from bloating, extract conditionally useful sections (e.g., end-to-end testing) into skills, which load only a short description by default and read full details on demand—progressive disclosure [2][3][7]. To teach agents how to create such skills, install the Anthropic-written 'skill creator' skill via the npx skills CLI, and be cautious about installing random skills because they can run arbitrary commands on your machine [3][7]. You can also store domain knowledge in markdown files to steer agent tool use and search behavior [6].

entries.question: What are the main themes across this corpus of videos?
entries.answer: The corpus splits into two overarching themes. One is AI-powered video/media processing: [1] and [2] describe splitting sports and wildlife footage into audio and transcripts, generating multimodal embeddings from both text and video frames, storing them in Elasticsearch, and using an ffmpeg amplitude spectrograph to detect audience cheering for highlight reels and then sending push notifications [1][2]. The other is crafting premium app/web experiences with AI: [3] and [8] showcase free UI component libraries like Skipper UI and liquid metal effects, [4][9][10] stress that great animations and illustrations require massive iteration (mixing styles, 30+ prompts, hand-drawn Procreate work) rather than one-shot generation, [5] says taste is the defining skill and premium is felt more than seen, and [7] highlights Whisper Flow for dictating iteration loops to AI agents.

entries.question: What are the recurring arguments the property videos make about the federal budget's tax changes?
entries.answer: The recurring arguments are that the changes amount to a "tax grab" dressed up as reform rather than a genuine fix [1][2]: marginal tax brackets were left unindexed so bracket creep pushes people into higher tax brackets [1], and investors describe the package as "definitely a tax grab" [2]. They argue the changes deliberately disincentivize existing properties to force buyers into new builds, using negative-gearing phase-outs and a reintroduced CGT indexation method [4][10], which they read as an admission the government isn't building enough [10]. They also argue the burden falls mainly on mum-and-dad and rent-vesting investors, while sophisticated investors can take the changes or leave them and find ways around them [2][3]. The videos repeat that the fundamentals haven't changed: population still needs housing, new builds remain unviable (30–50% of a house-and-land package cost is government taxes and charges), so the budget won't fix affordability [2][6]. They emphasize investors will find other mechanisms and any sentiment drop will be short-term [2]. They also stress public confusion: changes aren't immediate, deferral is different from forgiveness, the CGT discount still applies, and indexation is just a new calculation method [9]. A broader warning recurs that "everything is up for grabs" — homes, CGT waivers, and taxes could be targeted next [7]. Finally, they argue rents will rise far more than official estimates (e.g., ~$100/week compared with a $2/week prediction) [8].

entries.question: According to this corpus, how do senior engineers structure their agentic coding setups?
entries.answer: According to the corpus, the speakers describe agentic setups as a captain-and-crew structure: start with a core setup, recruit agents using memory and skills, work with a single agent, scale to multiple agents, and add a "first mate" to manage overhead [7]. Under the hood, they rely on an agentic loop where the model uses tools to search the codebase (and also general knowledge, markdown files, etc.), steered by additional instructions and domain knowledge [1]. They convert conditionally useful memory into skills—for example, extracting end-to-end testing instructions from agents.md into a project-level skill using Anthropic's skill creator and Vercel's npx skills CLI [3]. For multi-agent work, they use patterns such as creator-verifier (a fresh-context verifier is more likely to find issues), direct communication (hard to get right because state fragments), negotiation over shared resources, and broadcast [6]. At a workflow level, they reframe the software factory so an agent builds "the thing" instead of a person, while keeping orchestration, harness, sandbox, and model components in place [10]. They also emphasize context engineering and "own your context window" from the 12 Factor Agents paper [5]. Finally, they keep the human in charge: the agent should educate you with quizzes and visualizations and slow down when you lose grip, rather than running unattended [8], and human code review remains part of the loop [4].

entries.question: How did the property channels' stance on the budget's tax changes evolve across June 2026?
entries.answer: The retrieved transcript chunks do not document any evolution of the property channels' stance across June 2026. They provide static, post-budget analysis: negative gearing is not "gone" but changes are deferred, with properties bought after budget night receiving full negative gearing through the July 2027 tax return and only seeing a difference from July 2028 [2][4][8]; existing (grandfathered) properties keep their benefits [6]; and the budget also changed CGT indexation, trusts/bucket companies, and WATTO [1][6]. One chunk mentions "June, right now in 2026" only as an example of a property purchase date [8], not as a description of how commentary shifted over that month. Therefore, there is insufficient evidence to describe an evolution.

entries.answer: The retrieved chunks do not contain any information about Kun Chen's content evolving between June and July 2026. One chunk introduces Kun and his full agentic engineering workflow [9], and another outlines the chapters of that workflow (assembling the agent ship, recruiting crew mates, memory, skills, working with multiple agents, and adding a first mate) [5], but no dates or timeline are provided in the evidence.

entries.question: How do I make my resume ATS-friendly?
entries.answer: Use a clean, ATS-friendly template as a base, but don't stop there—a template alone isn't enough; you need keyword optimization [2]. Keep formatting simple: easy-to-read fonts (like Arial/Calibri), no images, charts, tables, headers/footers, emojis, colors/highlights, or columns, because complex layouts can confuse ATS parsers or be read out of order [6][4]. Keep margins consistent (one inch, or half an inch if you need more space), save the final file as PDF, and keep it to one page [1][4][9]. For the content, use an AI prompt to extract the 25 most important keywords from the job description, add the target job title at the top (or use it in your summary), and place those keywords in your key skills section and at the beginning of your bullet points [8][10][7][5].

entries.question: What should the professional summary at the top of a resume say?
entries.answer: The professional summary should be a short, thesis-like statement (1–2 sentences) that tells hiring managers who you are and what you bring to the table, so it can win them over in the first few seconds [3][8][10]. It should identify your role/title (e.g., marketing leader), your years of experience, and the environments you've worked in, then move into bragging about specific accomplishments with facts and figures [2][8]. It should be tailored to the specific job and not be generic boilerplate, and it should be written last so it truly summarizes the rest of your resume [6][8][10].

entries.question: How should I write my LinkedIn about section and skills so recruiters find me?
entries.answer: Write your About section as 3–4 concise paragraphs built from a keyword analysis: pull 5–10 relevant job descriptions into a word cloud generator and use the most frequent terms in your About text [1]. Follow a template: introduce yourself with years of experience, roles, and technologies; write a results-focused summary that uses numbers and data; and conclude with the types of opportunities you are looking for [1]. Avoid generic buzzwords like "motivated" or "rockstar"; instead state your title, skills, and specialization in a concise role + skill + interest + value format [3]. Put your target keywords in the About, Experience, and Skills sections, and upload your resume via Settings → Data Privacy → Job seeking preferences → Job application settings [2]. For the Skills section, add endorsed skills—LinkedIn only counts skills with at least one endorsement, and you need five endorsed skills to fully use the section—so choose five skills from your keyword analysis and ask colleagues/friends to endorse them [4]. You can also paste 2–3 job descriptions into an AI tool and ask it to list hard skills, technologies, job functions, industry terminology, and leadership skills while avoiding generic entry-level skills [7]. Finally, pin three skills in your experience section that reflect what you want to be known for, since this boosts discoverability [10]. Repeating your target role keyword in the header and bio also helps recruiters find you [6].

entries.question: What does a recruiter actually look for on an AI engineer resume?
entries.answer: Recruiters say they actually hunt for qualifications, not keywords. A skill only becomes a qualification when it appears in full sentences saying what you did, how you did it, the reason/result, and where you did it; a bare skill is just a keyword and won't get considered [2][10]. For AI engineer roles specifically, one recruiter lists: AI, LLM, NLP, Python (preferred; C/Java acceptable), agentic/AI architecture (LangChain, Crew, MCP, A2A), generative AI (e.g., RAG) or ML frameworks (TensorFlow/PyTorch), API design, Git/GitHub, cloud, NumPy, R, SDLC, CI/CD, DevOps, and explaining things to non-technical people, with roughly 75% of these needed — and they should not be dumped in a skill section [2]. Recruiters also screen for logistics like location, up-to-date info, visa/office availability, and whether the listed technologies genuinely match the job description [4]. Because recruiters spend about seven seconds on a resume, keeping it to one page and removing filler like knowing macOS/Windows or hobbies is important [9]. To get shortlisted, advice from AI professionals includes customizing the resume for the specific AI-engineer role, keeping to 6–8 solid skills, showing numbers/impact (e.g., improved accuracy, reduced inference time), and linking a well-structured GitHub for every serious project [6][3].

entries.question: How should I prepare for behavioural interview questions?
entries.answer: To prepare for behavioral interview questions, practice your answers out loud and prepare in advance by predicting likely questions and planning your responses [1][3]. Structure your answers using the STAR method — situation, task, action, result — so your impact is clear [1]. Build a reusable story bank of five or six stories that can be adapted across many questions; for example, the same story can answer a question about conflict or failure [1][5]. Use a behavioral questions template that includes common prompts such as "Why do you want to work here?", "Tell me about a time you disagreed with someone", "Tell me about a time you made a bold decision", and "Tell me about a time you solved a customer pain point" [2]. In the video, a Notion template was used to store answers and regenerate a fresh story bank from a work summary, which was then polished and practiced in front of a mirror or camera [2][6]. Keep a running note of interview questions you are asked and the answers you gave, so you can refine your bank over time [5]. Finally, prepare thoughtful questions to ask the interviewer at the end, such as what success looks like for a new hire or what the team finds most challenging [5].

entries.question: What advice do the job-search videos in this corpus repeat across resumes, LinkedIn and interviews?
entries.answer: Based only on the retrieved chunks, there is no single piece of advice that clearly repeats across resumes, LinkedIn, and interviews. The clearest repeated advice is for resumes and LinkedIn: tailor your materials to the specific job posting. For resumes, make the resume fit the job/team and avoid tech-stack mismatches with the job description, since mismatches can get the resume thrown out [9][10]. For LinkedIn, look closely at the job postings you're interested in, see what skills, tasks, software, and terminology they mention, and add the relevant ones to your skills section [7]. The chunks also suggest avoiding mass, conventional applications—[2] says the standard application route had a low success rate and a non-conventional approach led to a Google DeepMind interview, while [6] says the advice is not to reach out to recruiters on LinkedIn and apply to 50 jobs a day. However, none of the retrieved chunks contain actual advice for interviews; [1] only promises that interview preparation will be covered later in the video.
